title: Professional Sass Code Review
learning_outcomes: Explain professional sass code review and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply professional sass code review in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Professional Sass Code Review** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect reviewing naming and organization with reviewing selector specificity, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: The design problem is usually consistency across many related styles, not the ability to write shorter syntax. Combine semantic tokens, a clear module boundary, reusable component patterns, and CSS-native runtime features where each has a distinct role.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Design the public interface for the next developer: document tokens and arguments, keep internals private, compile from a documented entrypoint, and demonstrate the result in a small consumer page.

items.title: Reviewing naming and organization
items.text: For reviewing naming and organization, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

items.title: Reviewing selector specificity
items.text: Predict the expanded selector before compiling. Keep nesting shallow and verify that the emitted selector does not match more elements than intended.

items.title: Checking for deprecated Sass features
items.text: Migrate incrementally, prefer current Dart Sass modules, inspect warnings, and compare before/after CSS. Automated migration still requires code review and tests.

items.title: Evaluating generated CSS size
items.text: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact.

items.title: Reviewing responsive and accessible behavior
items.text: Sass emits the at-rule; the browser evaluates its condition at runtime. Confirm that the output contains the intended query and test the interface at real viewport or feature conditions.

items.title: Documenting decisions and preparing releases
items.text: For documenting decisions and preparing releases, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates professional sass code review. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Professional Sass Code Review
content_blocks.code: Review checklist: names and module boundaries; selector specificity; deprecated constructs; compiled CSS size; responsive behavior; keyboard focus; release notes.
content_blocks.expected_output: A code review checks both source maintainability and the CSS emitted for the browser.
content_blocks.execution_note: This course example is a Sass/SCSS or tooling example. CodeLeaf’s current in-browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; compile Sass locally with Dart Sass. Do not treat the browser preview as a Sass compiler.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates professional sass code review. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates professional sass code review. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.

summary: Professional Sass Code Review is useful when it solves the specific organization or reuse problem described in this lesson.
Keep compile-time Sass behavior distinct from browser-time CSS behavior.
Validate both source intent and generated CSS before relying on the pattern in a larger project.
